anchors.fact: Under a 1919 treaty that limited cheap foreign spirits, local distilling in Nigeria was banned, and ogogoro stayed illegal after independence in 1960 (Oxford, OGOGORO pdf 1417). **The ban's start year is contested** (PUNCH 2022: "an era of prohibition that began in 1910"), so the reading gives no start year beyond Oxford's treaty, and never says imports flooded in.
anchors.meaning: One rule for the foreign spirit and another for the local one. The unfair thing that "those are the rules" kept standing.
anchors.speaksTo: the unfair thing; Wren's fear (told to leave it to the people in charge)

anchors.fact: In 1968 the educator and activist Tai Solarin (1922–1994), a teetotaller, "contrived to get himself arrested for possessing the spirit", to dramatise the injustice of banning a local spirit while allowing foreign ones (Oxford pdf 1417). The motive is Oxford's, relayed from its 1968 newspaper source. **Only what he did; nothing he said or wrote.**
anchors.meaning: Not their fight, broken where everyone could see who did it. His not drinking shows he had nothing to gain from it, never a virtue.
anchors.speaksTo: test 1, 2; the one true thing ("It's rarely your fight")

anchors.fact: He was charged: "Solarin Freed of Gin Charge", *Lagos Daily Times*, 14 Sep 1968, p. 3 (cited in Oxford's bibliography, pdf 1418; the paper itself is unread). The charge was printed as "gin". **No place, no arrest date, no sentence, no time in a cell is on any page**: never "risked prison", never a police station. The 14th is the paper's date, not the day he was freed.
anchors.meaning: The cost was his, and it was meant to be seen. He paid for doing something instead of doing nothing.
anchors.speaksTo: test 4; "You'd rather pay for doing something…"

anchors.fact: "That finally changed in 1968, when" he did it (Oxford pdf 1417). **Cause at "when" strength, no stronger**; no law and no date of the change. Contested by secondaries that date legality to independence (PUNCH 2022; Olúpàyímọ, *Yoruba Studies Review* 2017, pp. 204–205) or "the early 1960s" (*Vanguard* 2015). The 1968 gin charge shows the ban was still enforced in 1968, so Oxford stands, at its own strength.
anchors.meaning: It worked: it broke for everyone, not one case at a time. Also what they give: a rule shown to be movable.
anchors.speaksTo: test 3; the position (break it once, where it's seen, so it breaks for everyone)

anchors.fact: Ogogoro, also called "local gin", is Nigeria's national spirit, distilled from the sap of the raffia or oil palm (Oxford pdf 1417). Gin was "the preferred spirit around the Gulf of Guinea" (same page). PUNCH (Adaorah Oduah, 29 Jul 2022) says the British smeared it as a "knockoff" of British gin: **secondary, a guard for the reading, not a fact for it** unless attributed.
anchors.meaning: The local spirit was never a copy of anything.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink; Wren's guard (fairness, not victory)

anchors.fact: Pedro's Premium Ògógóró: 40%, unaged, distilled from fermented palm sap in villages in Delta and Ogun states, then redistilled in Lagos (*Difford's Guide*, product page, fetched 2026-10-01). £58.95 per 50 cl (Artifex Drinks, fetched 2026-10-01). Stocked in Lagos, London, Nairobi and Accra (PUNCH 2022). Founded by Lola Pedro and Chibu Akukwe in 2017, first bottle on sale 2019 (PUNCH). **There's also a 5-year aged version (Artifex): the spec names the unaged one.** Difford's taste notes include coconut, but they describe flavour, not an ingredient.
anchors.meaning: Buyable, branded and made properly. Recommended, never unbranded (the safety guard).

anchors.fact: Splitting a Martini's base between spirits keeps its form (*Cocktail Codex* p. 71, Dean Martin; the Vesper on the same page splits gin with vodka). **The Codex's splits are unequal; equal halves are ours.**
anchors.meaning: Gin and the local spirit at the same measure: one rule for both, neither taking the other's seat. The twist, tied to the story in one clause. Near *One Table*'s equal thirds (rye and cognac, the Vieux Carré): owned in Checks; theirs is two sides at the same weight, ours one rule for both.
anchors.speaksTo: the drink as proof; Wren r1 (equals side by side)

cocktail.closingLine: Equal measures, no more of either. Then pick the rule that isn't fair, and break it where it can be seen.
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
Measure 30 ml of the ogogoro and 30 ml of the gin into a mixing glass or a jar.
Add the vermouth, the half barspoon of demerara syrup and the dash of orange bitters.
Fill with ice and stir for 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the mixing glass feels very cold.
Empty the glass, strain the drink into it, then squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Can't Watch

recipe.note: a Nigerian spirit distilled from palm sap, 40%. Buy the unaged Premium, not the 5-year aged bottling. If you can't find it: another branded, unaged West African palm-sap spirit, never a homemade or unlabelled one
any London dry gin of 40% or more
one part demerara sugar dissolved in one part warm water, cooled

cocktail.tagline: It's rarely your fight. That's never once stopped you.

reading.epigraph: In 1968, a non-drinker got himself arrested for one of the spirits in this glass.
whoYouAre: Someone sighs: it's a pity, but those are the rules. You've already stopped listening. You're working out which rule it is, who it's really for, and what it would take to get round it by Friday. Not for you. Usually it isn't even your fight.

People put it down to nerve, or a taste for trouble. It's neither. It's that you can't watch. Being told to wait, to go through the proper channels, to leave it to the people who run things while it carries on happening: that's the thing that truly frightens you. And there's a part you'd never say out loud: some of it is for you. Doing something, even something that costs you, is how you stop feeling helpless.

So you fix it, quietly, one person at a time: a rule bent just for them, a back way found. It works. What it gives people is real: with you around, "those are the rules" stops being the end of the matter, and that matters more than you let yourself think. But you know the other half. The rule is still there in the morning, and so is the next person it lands on.
yours: For decades, Nigeria's own spirit was against the law. Ogogoro is distilled from the sap of palm trees. In colonial Nigeria a treaty banned distilling spirits locally, while foreign spirits could still be sold, gin above all. People made it anyway, more and more of them, and it stayed illegal even after independence in 1960.

In 1968, a Nigerian educator called Tai Solarin got himself arrested for having some. He did it on purpose, to show everyone how unfair it was to ban a local spirit and allow foreign ones. That September, a Lagos paper's headline read "Solarin Freed of Gin Charge". The ban ended that same year. And Tai Solarin didn't drink.

How it went, we don't know. I like to think he simply made the rule do, where everyone could see, the one thing it couldn't defend. It was never his drink. He picked the fight up anyway, and made sure the charge landed on him. I recognise you in that. If putting it right has to cost somebody, you'd rather it cost you.

The cocktail I've made for you is built like a Martini, the classic that needs no introduction: stirred, ice-cold and strong, poured into a little stemmed glass, chilled first. It stands on two spirits in equal measure: Pedro's, a Nigerian ogogoro distilled from palm sap in villages and then again in Lagos, and a London dry gin. Thirty millilitres of each, and neither stands in for the other. I split them as a nod to the point Tai Solarin got himself arrested to make: one rule for both, so neither gets the bigger share, the way you'd always have it. Sweet vermouth brings them together, with a little demerara syrup, which sits well with the toffee tasters find in Pedro's, and a dash of orange bitters. The orange oils, pressed from the peel above the glass, belong to both.

You'll go on fixing things one person at a time, and you should. But once, pick the rule that keeps sending you back, and stop working round it on the quiet. Do it where people can see who did it, so the rule has to answer for itself. Not for the thanks. So it changes for everyone, and you get the thing you've wanted all along: never having to watch that one again.
